19       Plaintiff Kimera Labs Inc. (“Plaintiff”) brings this lawsuit against Defendants Raj 
20  Jayashankar (“Jayashankar”), Exocel Bio Inc. (“Exocel”), Alejandro Contreras 
21  (“Contreras”), Deb Hubers (“Hubers”), and Craig Evan Winkels (“Winkels”)  
22  (collectively, “Defendants”), alleging misappropriation of Plaintiff’s trade secrets, civil 
23  conspiracy to commit tortious interference with business relations, tortious interference 
24  with business relations, unjust enrichment, and unfair competition.  See Doc. No. 31.  On 
25  June 6, 2022, Defendants Jayashankar, Exocel, Contreras, and Hubers filed a motion to 
26  dismiss Plaintiff’s First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) in its entirety pursuant to Federal 
27  Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).  Doc. No. 40.  On June 17, 2022, Defendant Winkels 
28  filed a separate motion to dismiss Plaintiff’s FAC for lack of personal jurisdiction 
1  pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(2), or in the alternative, a motion to 
2  dismiss for failure to state a claim pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).  
3  Doc. No. 41.  Plaintiff opposed both motions.  See Doc. Nos. 42, 45.  Defendants filed 
4  replies.  See Doc. Nos. 44, 47.  The Court found the matters suitable for determination on 
5  the papers and without oral argument pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 78(b) 
6  and Civil Local Rule 7.1.d.1.  See Doc. Nos. 46, 48.  For the reasons set forth below, the 
7  Court GRANTS Defendants’ motions to dismiss with leave to amend.          
8                              I. BACKGROUND1                                
9       Plaintiff, a corporation based in Florida, is “an FDA-registered tissue processing 
10  laboratory that specializes in scientific research focusing on exosome characterization 
11  and placental mesenchymal stem cell exosomes production and optimization.”  FAC ¶¶ 1, 
12  6.  Plaintiff invested heavily in developing a “proprietary method of exosome isolation” 
13  in order to produce XoGlo, “the first clinically available exosome product in the world.”  
14  Id. ¶¶ 1, 27.  Plaintiff also spent “a substantial amount of time, expense, and effort” 
15  creating a customer list.  Id. ¶ 33.                                      
16       Plaintiff required its employees to maintain confidentiality regarding its customer 
17  list and its process used to develop XoGlo, and included such requirements in their 
18  employment agreements.  See id. ¶ 17.  Dr. Melissa Selinger (“Dr. Selinger”) was 
19  employed by Plaintiff from 2018 to 2019.  Id. ¶ 20.  Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Selinger and 
20  Defendants “brazenly and secretly engaged in corporate espionage” in order to establish 
21  Exocel, a business that “directly competes against [Plaintiff] in the exosome isolation 
22  industry using [Plaintiff]’s trade secrets and other confidential information to 
23  manufacture and sell” Exovex, a “competing extracellular vesicle/exosome product[].”

12                               II. DISCUSSION                               
13  A.   Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Personal Jurisdiction                  
14       The Court first addresses Defendant Winkels’s motion to dismiss pursuant to Rule 
15  12(b)(2).2  See Doc. No. 41.                                              
16       1.   Legal Standard                                                  
17       “Federal courts ordinarily follow state law in determining the bounds of their 
18  jurisdiction over persons.”  Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117, 125 (2014).  Because 
19  “California’s long-arm statute allows the exercise of personal jurisdiction to the full 
20  extent permissible under the U.S. Constitution,” the court’s inquiry centers on whether 
21  exercising jurisdiction comports with due process.  Picot v. Weston, 780 F.3d 1206, 1211 
22  (9th Cir. 2015) (quoting Daimler AG, 571 U.S. at 125); see also Cal. Civ. Proc. Code 
23  § 410.10 (“A court of this state may exercise jurisdiction on any basis not inconsistent 
24  with the Constitution of this state or of the United States.”).  Due process requires that the 
25  defendant “have certain minimum contacts” with the forum state “such that the 
26                                                                            
27                                                                            
28                                                                            
1  maintenance of the suit does not offend ‘traditional notions of fair play and substantial 
2  justice.’”  Int’l Shoe Co. v. Wash., 326 U.S. 310, 316 (1945) (quoting Milliken v. Meyer, 
3  311 U.S. 457, 463 (1940)).                                                
4       Depending on the strength of those contacts, there are two forms that personal 
5  jurisdiction may take: general and specific.  Boschetto v. Hansing, 539 F.3d 1011, 1016 
6  (9th Cir. 2008).  Here, Plaintiff does not allege that Defendant Winkels is subject to 
7  general jurisdiction in California; instead, it alleges that specific jurisdiction exists.  See 
8  FAC ¶ 11; Doc. No. 45 at 9–14.3  When a plaintiff relies on specific jurisdiction, he must 
9  establish that jurisdiction is proper for “each claim asserted against a defendant.”  Picot, 
10  780 F.3d at 1211 (quoting Action Embroidery Corp. v. Atl. Embroidery, Inc., 368 F.3d 
11  1174, 1180 (9th Cir. 2004)).  If personal jurisdiction exists over one claim, but not others, 
12  the court may exercise pendent personal jurisdiction over any remaining claims that arise 
13  out of the same “common nucleus of operative facts” as the claim for which jurisdiction 
14  exists.  Id. (quoting Action Embroidery Corp., 368 F.3d at 1181).         
15       A three-part test is used to assess whether a defendant has sufficient contacts with 
16  the forum state to be subject to specific personal jurisdiction:          
17                                                                            
        (1)  The  non-resident  defendant  must  purposefully  direct  his  activities  or 
18                                                                            
        consummate some transaction with the forum or resident thereof; or perform 
19       some  act  by  which  he  purposefully  avails  himself  of  the  privilege  of 
        conducting  activities  in  the  forum,  thereby  invoking  the  benefits  and 
20                                                                            
        protections of its laws;                                             
21                                                                            
        (2) the claim must be one which arises out of or relates to the defendant’s 
22                                                                            
        forum-related activities; and                                        
23                                                                            
        (3) the exercise of jurisdiction must comport with fair play and substantial 
24                                                                            
        justice, i.e., it must be reasonable.                                
25                                                                            
26                                                                            
27                                                                            
28                                                                            
1  Schwarzenegger v. Fred Martin Motor Co., 374 F.3d 797, 802 (9th Cir. 2004).  The 
2  plaintiff has the burden of proving the first two prongs.  CollegeSource, Inc. v. 
3  AcademyOne, Inc., 653 F.3d 1066, 1076 (9th Cir. 2011).  If he does so, the burden shifts 
4  to the defendant to “set forth a ‘compelling case’ that the exercise of jurisdiction would 
5  not be reasonable.”  Id. (quoting Burger King Corp. v. Rudzewicz, 471 U.S. 462, 477 
6  (1985)).                                                                  
7       The exact form of jurisdictional inquiry depends on the nature of the claims at 
8  issue.  Picot, 780 F.3d at 1212.  For claims sounding in contract, courts generally apply a 
9  “purposeful availment” analysis and ask whether a defendant has “purposefully avail[ed] 
10  [himself] of the privilege of conducting activities within the forum State, thus invoking 
11  the benefits and protections of its laws.”  Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 802 (quoting 
12  Hanson v. Denckla, 357 U.S. 235, 253 (1958)).  For claims sounding in tort, courts 
13  instead apply a “purposeful direction” test and look to evidence that the defendant has 
14  directed his actions at the forum state, even if those actions took place elsewhere.  Id. at 
15  802–03.  Here, Plaintiff asserts tort claims against Defendant Winkels.  FAC ¶¶ 15–56. 
16       In analyzing whether a court has specific personal jurisdiction over a tort claim, the 
17  Ninth Circuit applies the three-part “effects” test derived from Calder v. Jones, 465 U.S. 
18  783 (1984) (the “Calder test”).  Picot, 780 F.3d at 1213–14 (citing Schwarzenegger, 374 
19  F.3d at 803).  Under this test, a defendant purposefully directed his activities at the forum 
20  if he: “(1) committed an intentional act, (2) expressly aimed at the forum state, 
21  (3) causing harm that the defendant knows is likely to be suffered in the forum state.”  Id.  
22  (quoting Dole Food Co. v. Watts, 303 F.3d 1104, 1111 (9th Cir. 2002)).  In applying this 
23  test, courts must “look[] to the defendant’s contacts with the forum State itself, not the 
24  defendant’s contacts with persons who reside there.”  Walden v. Fiore, 571 U.S. 277, 285 
25  (2014).  Thus, a “mere injury to a forum resident is not a sufficient connection to the 
26  forum.”  Id. at 290.  Rather, “an injury is jurisdictionally relevant only insofar as it shows 
27  that the defendant has formed a contact with the forum State.”  Id.       
28                                                                            
1       The meaning of the term “intentional act” in the court’s jurisdictional analysis is 
2  essentially the same as in the context of intentional torts; namely, the defendant must act 
3  with the “intent to perform an actual, physical act in the real world.”  Picot, 780 F.3d at 
4  1214 (quoting Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 806).  The second prong of the test, “express 
5  aiming,” asks whether the defendant’s allegedly tortious action was “expressly aimed at 
6  the forum.”  Brayton Purcell LLP v. Recordon & Recordon, 606 F.3d 1124, 1129 (9th 
7  Cir. 2010).  As to this prong, the exact nature of the court’s analysis varies from case to 
8  case and “depends, to a significant degree, on the specific type of tort or other wrongful 
9  conduct at issue.”  Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 807.                      
10       2.   Analysis                                                        
11       Here, Defendant Winkels only challenges the first prong of the test for specific 
12  jurisdiction.  Doc. No. 41-1 at 7–11.  Therefore, the Court focuses its analysis on the 
13  Calder test to determine whether Winkels purposefully directed his activities at 
14  California.                                                               
15       The Court first addresses the second factor of the Calder test: whether Defendant 
16  Winkels’s alleged conduct was expressly aimed at California.  Winkels argues that the 
17  Court lacks specific jurisdiction because Plaintiff “fails to allege any connection between 
18  Winkels and California, let alone in a ‘meaningful way.’”  Id. at 10.  In response, Plaintiff 
19  generally argues that Winkels is subject to specific personal jurisdiction in California 
20  because “[t]he violations of law at issue in this lawsuit were conducted by Winkels within 
21  this Court’s [Southern District of California] judicial jurisdiction.”  Doc. No. 45 at 12.   
22       Plaintiff alleges that Defendants, including Winkels, conspired with Dr. Selinger 
23  “to help create a business [Exocel] that they intended to directly compete against 
24  [Plaintiff] by using [Plaintiff]’s [trade secrets].  Defendants, including Winkels, worked 
25  with Dr. Selinger to extract [Plaintiff]’s [trade secrets] and promote the Exocel Project to 
26  potential investors.”  FAC ¶¶ 22, 39.  Plaintiff further contends that Defendants, 
27  including Winkels, misappropriated Plaintiff’s trade secrets by accepting, disclosing to 
28  Exocel, retaining, and using Plaintiff’s trade secrets.  Id. ¶¶ 28, 44.  According to 
1  Plaintiff, Winkels “assisted with the planning for the competing company and conferred 
2  and conspired with Dr. Selinger to seal [Plaintiff’s standard operating procedures] and 
3  other confidential information.”  Id. ¶ 53.  And Plaintiff maintains that Defendant 
4  Winkels aimed to profit from the conspiracy to steal from Plaintiff and use the stolen 
5  information to create and operate Exocel, a Delaware corporation with its principal place 
6  of business in San Diego County, California.  Id. ¶¶ 7, 55.               
7       As an initial matter, many of the allegations listed above pertain to Defendants, 
8  collectively, and Plaintiff does not separate out each Defendants’ actions in the 
9  challenged conduct.  This is improper.  See Head v. Las Vegas Sands, LLC, 298 F. Supp. 
10  3d 963, 973 (S.D. Tex. 2018) (“[A] plaintiff must submit evidence supporting personal 
11  jurisdiction over each defendant, and cannot simply lump them all together”) (citing 
12  Calder, 465 U.S. at 790) (“Each defendant’s contacts with the forum State must be 
13  assessed individually.”).                                                 
14       Plaintiff’s claims against Defendant Winkels include two counts of   
15  misappropriation of Plaintiff’s trade secrets in violation of the DTSA and one count of 
16  civil conspiracy to commit tortious interference with business relations (Counts I, II, and 
17  III).  As stated above, “[p]ersonal jurisdiction must exist for each claim asserted against a 
18  defendant.”  Action Embroidery Corp., 368 F.3d at 1180.  The only allegations in the 
19  FAC that refer to Defendant Winkels individually include Plaintiff’s general assertions 
20  that “[t]his Court has personal jurisdiction over Winkels because the violations of law at 
21  issue in this lawsuit were conducted by Winkels within this Court’s judicial district,” 
22  FAC ¶ 11, “Winkels assisted the financing part of the competing business,” id. ¶¶ 22, 39, 
23  and “Winkels assisted with planning for the competing company and conferred and 
24  conspired with Dr. Selinger to steal [Plaintiff’s] [standard operating procedures] and 
25  other confidential information,” id. ¶ 53.  Indeed, Plaintiff fails to provide specific 
26  allegations showing that Winkels’s acts as to each count above were expressly aimed at 
27  California.  Plaintiff is a Florida corporation doing business in Florida.  FAC ¶ 6.  
28  Defendant Winkels (1) resided in Illinois during the years relevant to this lawsuit; 
1  (2) currently resides in Ohio; (3) never resided in California; and (4) does not have any 
2  personal or professional connections to California.  Doc. No. 41-2 at 2.  Without more 
3  specific facts, the Court finds that Plaintiff has not met its burden of showing how 
4  Defendant Winkels’s alleged conduct—misappropriating trade secrets and conspiring to 
5  interfere with the business relations of a Florida corporation doing business in Florida—
6  was expressly aimed at California.  See Professional’s Choice Sports Medicine Prods., 
7  Inc. v. Hegeman, No. 15-cv-2505-BAS (WVG), 2016 WL 1450704, at *4 (S.D. Cal. 
8  April 12, 2016) (“[A] plaintiff must point to contacts which demonstrate that the 
9  defendant ‘expressly aimed its tortious conduct at the forum.’”).         
10       Because Plaintiff has not satisfied the expressly aiming element of the Calder test, 
11  the Court need not address any of the other prongs because “[f]ailing to sufficiently plead 
12  any one of these three elements [from Calder] is fatal to Plaintiff’s attempt to show 
13  personal jurisdiction.”  Rupert v. Bond, 68 F. Supp. 3d 1142, 1163 (N.D. Cal. 2014) 
14  (citing Brayton Purcell LLP, 606 F.3d at 1128–29).  As such, the Court declines to reach 
15  the remaining specific jurisdiction requirements, i.e., whether Plaintiff’s claim arises out 
16  of or relates to Defendant’s forum-related activities and whether the exercise of 
17  jurisdiction would comport with fair play and substantial justice.        
18       In sum, the Court GRANTS Defendant Winkels’s motion to dismiss for lack of 
19  personal jurisdiction with leave to amend.4  See McKesson HBOC, Inc. v. N.Y. State 
20  Common Ret. Fund, Inc., 339 F.3d 1087, 1090 (9th Cir. 2003) (noting that in the event of 
21  a jurisdictional defect, dismissal without leave to amend is proper only if it is clear that 
22  the complaint could not be saved by any amendment).

1  B.   Motion to Dismiss for Failure to State a Claim                       
2       Next, the Court addresses the remaining Defendants’ motion to dismiss pursuant to 
3  Rule 12(b)(6).  See Doc. No. 40.                                          
4       1.   Legal Standard                                                  
5       A Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss tests the sufficiency of the complaint.  Navarro 
6  v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001).  A pleading must contain “a short and plain 
7  statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
8  8(a)(2).  However, plaintiffs must also plead “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is 
9  plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); see also 
10  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6).  The plausibility standard demands more than a “formulaic 
11  recitation of the elements of a cause of action,” or “‘naked assertions’ devoid of ‘further 
12  factual enhancement.’”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Twombly, 
13  550 U.S. at 555, 557).  Instead, the complaint “must contain sufficient allegations of 
14  underlying facts to give fair notice and to enable the opposing party to defend itself 
15  effectively.”  Starr v. Baca, 652 F.3d 1202, 1216 (9th Cir. 2011).        
16       In reviewing a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), courts must assume the truth 
17  of all factual allegations and must construe them in the light most favorable to the 
18  nonmoving party.  Cahill v. Liberty Mut. Ins. Co., 80 F.3d 336, 337–38 (9th Cir. 1996) 
19  (citing Nat’l Wildlife Fed'n v. Espy, 45 F.3d 1337, 1340 (9th Cir. 1995)).  The court need 
20  not take legal conclusions as true merely because they are cast in the form of factual 
21  allegations.  Roberts v. Corrothers, 812 F.2d 1173, 1177 (9th Cir. 1987) (quoting W. Min. 
22  Council v. Watt, 643 F.2d 618, 624 (9th Cir. 1981)).  Similarly, “conclusory allegations 
23  of law and unwarranted inferences are not sufficient to defeat a motion to dismiss.”  
24  Pareto v. FDIC, 139 F.3d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 1998).                        
25       In determining the propriety of a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, courts generally may not 
26  look beyond the complaint for additional facts.  See United States v. Ritchie, 342 F.3d 
27  903, 907–08 (9th Cir. 2003).  “A court may, however, consider certain materials—
28  documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the 
1  complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a 
2  motion for summary judgment.”  Id.; see also Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 
3  688 (9th Cir. 2001), overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County Of Santa Clara, 
4  307 F.3d 1119, 1125–26 (9th Cir. 2002).  “However, [courts] are not required to accept as 
5  true conclusory allegations which are contradicted by documents referred to in the 
6  complaint.”  Steckman v. Hart Brewing, Inc., 143 F.3d 1293, 1295–96 (9th Cir. 1998) 
7  (citing In re Stac Electronics Securities Litigation, 89 F.3d 1399, 1403 (9th Cir. 1996)). 
8       Where dismissal is appropriate, a court should grant leave to amend unless the 
9  plaintiff could not possibly cure the defects in the pleading.  Knappenberger v. City of 
10  Phoenix, 566 F.3d 936, 942 (9th Cir. 2009) (quoting Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1127 
11  (9th Cir. 2000)).                                                         
12       2.   Trade Secret Misappropriation                                   
13       Because this Court’s jurisdiction over the remaining Defendants is based on federal 
14  question jurisdiction, see FAC ¶ 3, the Court begins by addressing the sufficiency of 
15  Plaintiff’s federal claims.5                                              
16       Plaintiff’s first and second causes of action are for trade secret misappropriation in 
17  violation of the DTSA.  See FAC ¶¶ 15–18.  Plaintiff alleges that Defendants 
18  misappropriated its “proprietary method of growing, harvesting, and isolating exosomes 
19  derived from placental mesenchymal stem cells for use in human therapeutic products” 
20  (“Kimera’s Process”) and its customer list.  FAC ¶ 16.  Defendants argue that these 
21  claims should be dismissed because Plaintiff does not allege ownership of its trade 
22  secrets with particularity and “fail[s] to put Defendants and the Court on notice of the 
23  boundaries of [Plaintiff]’s claims.”  Doc. No. 40 at 18.  Defendants also argue that 
24  Plaintiff “fails to plausibly allege misappropriation.”  Id. at 22–24.  In response, Plaintiff

2  them.”  Doc. No. 42 at 12.  In addition, Plaintiff argues that its “allegations, and all

6            a.   Applicable Law                                             
7       To plead a trade secret misappropriation cause of action under the DTSA, a 
8  plaintiff must allege the following: “(1) the plaintiff owned a trade secret; (2) the 
9  defendant misappropriated the trade secret; and (3) the defendant’s actions damaged the 
10  plaintiff.”  AlterG, Inc. v. Boost Treadmills LLC, 388 F. Supp. 3d 1133, 1144 (N.D. Cal. 
11  2019) (quoting Alta Devices, Inc. v. LG Elecs., Inc., 343 F. Supp. 3d 868, 877 (N.D. Cal. 
12  2018)).  The DTSA provides for a private cause of action for owners of trade secrets that 
13  are misappropriated “if the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or 
14  intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce.”  18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1).  The DTSA 
15  defines “trade secret” as “all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, 
16  economic, or engineering information, including patterns, plans, compilations, program 
17  devices, formulas, designs, prototypes, methods, techniques, processes, procedures, 
18  programs, or codes, whether tangible or intangible, and whether or how stored, compiled, 
19  or memorialized physically, electronically, graphically, photographically, or in writing” 
20  so long as the owner (a) “has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret” 
21  and (b) “derives independent economic value” from being secret.  18 U.S.C. § 1839(3).  
22  Under the DTSA “misappropriation” is the “(a) ‘acquisition of a trade secret’ by a person 
23  who knows or should know the secret was improperly acquired or (b) ‘disclosure or use 
24  of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent.’”  Cave Consulting Grp., 
25  Inc. v. Truven Health Analytics Inc., No. 15-CV-02177-SI, 2017 WL 1436044, at *3 
26  (N.D. Cal. Apr. 24, 2017) (quoting 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)).  In sum, the DTSA 
27  “contemplates three theories of liability: (1) acquisition, (2) disclosure, or (3) use.”  Id. at 
28  *4 (citing 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)).                                          
1       Defendants argue Plaintiff fails to allege its trade secrets with “sufficient 
2  particularity.”  Doc. No. 40 at 13.  However, in applying the Rule 12(b)(6) standard to 
3  DTSA allegations, the Court applies Rule 8’s general pleading standards, which require 
4  plausibility as opposed to particularity.  Defendants cite to Soil Retention Products, Inc. 
5  v. Brentwood Industries, Inc., 512 F. Supp. 3d 929, 965 (S.D. Cal. 2021), which applies 
6  the heightened pleading standard of “particularity” from the California Uniform Trade 
7  Secrets Act (“CUTSA”).  Here, Plaintiff does not plead any claims under CUTSA, and 
8  the Court finds that the DTSA does not incorporate CUTSA’s pleading standard requiring 
9  particularity.  See Physician’s Surrogacy, Inc. v. German, No. 17CV0718-MMA (WVG), 
10  2017 WL 3622329, at *9 (S.D. Cal. Aug. 23, 2017) (citing David Bohrer, Threatened 
11  Misappropriation of Trade Secrets: Making A Federal (DTSA) Case Out of It, 33 Santa 
12  Clara High Tech. L.J. 506, 521 (2017)); see also Power Integrations, Inc. v. De Lara, No. 
13  20-cv-410-MMA (MSB), 2020 WL 1467406, at *17 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 26, 2020) (applying 
14  a Rule 8 standard where there were only DTSA claims at issue); but see AlterG, Inc., 388 
15  F. Supp. 3d at 1144 n.1 (applying a Rule 9(b) standard).  Although “elements of a trade 
16  secret misappropriation claim under the DTSA are substantially similar to those under 
17  older state statutes,” such as CUTSA, Vendavo, Inc. v. Price f(x) AG, No. 17-CV-06930-
18  RS, 2018 WL 1456697, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 23, 2018), the similarity pertains to the 
19  substantive elements and does not pertain to the procedural pleading standard.  Thus, 
20  absent any explicit language in the DTSA requiring a heightened pleading standard or 
21  allegations of fraud or mistake, the Court finds that it must apply the general rules of 
22  pleading under Rule 8.                                                    
23            b.   Ownership of Trade Secret                                  
24                 i.   Kimera’s Process                                      
25       Defendants argue that as to Kimera’s Process, Plaintiff only puts forth “surface 
26  allegations” and “fails to notify Defendants what about Kimera’s Process actually has 
27  potential to be trade secret.”  Doc. No. 40 at 19– 20.  In response, Plaintiff argues that it 
28  “identified and described the Kimera Process with sufficient particularity to separate it 
1  from matters of general knowledge in the trade and of special knowledge of those persons 
2  skilled in the trade and to permit Defendants to ascertain the boundaries within which it 
3  lies.”  Doc. No. 42 at 17.                                                
4       As stated above, the Court must determine whether Plaintiff’s pleading of its 
5  DTSA claims plausibly express “a short and plain statement of the claim.”  Fed. R. Civ. 
6  P. 8(a)(2); see also Twombly, 550 U.S. at 570 (“[W]e do not require heightened fact 
7  pleading of specifics, but only enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on 
8  its face.”).  The Court finds that Plaintiff has met this requirement as to the Kimera 
9  Process.                                                                  
10       First, Plaintiff alleges the following paragraph pertaining to the Kimera Process:

        an industrial scale, clinically therapeutic exosome products for humans in a

15       harvesting, and isolating exosomes derived from placental mesenchymal stem

5       A Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss tests the sufficiency of the complaint.  Navarro 
6  v. Block,
250 F.3d 729, 732
 (9th Cir. 2001).  A pleading must contain “a short and plain 
7  statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
8  8(a)(2).  However, plaintiffs must also plead “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is 
9  plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly,
550 U.S. 544, 570
 (2007); see also 
10  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6).  The plausibility standard demands more than a “formulaic 
11  recitation of the elements of a cause of action,” or “‘naked assertions’ devoid of ‘further 
12  factual enhancement.’”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (quoting Twombly, 
13
550 U.S. at 555, 557
).  Instead, the complaint “must contain sufficient allegations of 
14  underlying facts to give fair notice and to enable the opposing party to defend itself 
15  effectively.”  Starr v. Baca,
652 F.3d 1202, 1216
 (9th Cir. 2011).        
16       In reviewing a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), courts must assume the truth 
17  of all factual allegations and must construe them in the light most favorable to the 
18  nonmoving party.  Cahill v. Liberty Mut. Ins. Co.,
80 F.3d 336
, 337–38 (9th Cir. 1996) 
19  (citing Nat’l Wildlife Fed'n v. Espy,
45 F.3d 1337
, 1340 (9th Cir. 1995)).  The court need 
20  not take legal conclusions as true merely because they are cast in the form of factual 
21  allegations.  Roberts v. Corrothers,
812 F.2d 1173, 1177
 (9th Cir. 1987) (quoting W. Min. 
22  Council v. Watt,
643 F.2d 618
, 624 (9th Cir. 1981)).  Similarly, “conclusory allegations 
23  of law and unwarranted inferences are not sufficient to defeat a motion to dismiss.”  
24  Pareto v. FDIC,
139 F.3d 696, 699
 (9th Cir. 1998).                        
25       In determining the propriety of a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, courts generally may not 
26  look beyond the complaint for additional facts.  See United States v. Ritchie,
342 F.3d 27 903
, 907–08 (9th Cir. 2003).  “A court may, however, consider certain materials—
28  documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the 
1  complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a 
2  motion for summary judgment.”  Id.; see also Lee v. City of Los Angeles,
250 F.3d 668

4
307 F.3d 1119
, 1125–26 (9th Cir. 2002).  “However, [courts] are not required to accept as
